title: Sievert vs Gray vs Rem vs Rad: Radiation Dose Explained
h1: Radiation dose units — sievert, gray, rem, rad
description: 1 Gy = 100 rad = absorbed dose. 1 Sv = 100 rem = equivalent dose weighted by radiation type. Confuse them and dose limits go out by 20×.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: Absorbed dose is energy per kg. Equivalent dose weights by biological damage. Effective dose weights again by organ sensitivity. Three different physical quantities, one unit family.
body: Radiation protection uses three related but distinct dose quantities. Each has an SI and a legacy unit. Mixing them by name has produced medical dosing errors that hit the news.

> Absorbed dose: 1 Gy (gray) = 1 J/kg = 100 rad
> Equivalent dose: 1 Sv (sievert) = Σ w_R × D = 100 rem
> w_R = 1 for photons/electrons, 20 for alpha, 5–20 for neutrons

Gy (or rad): what the tissue absorbs — used in radiotherapy. Sv (or rem): biologically-weighted, used for occupational and public dose limits. Effective dose (also Sv): further weighted by organ sensitivity, used for whole-body risk.
Natural background: 2–3 mSv/year. Chest X-ray: 0.1 mSv. CT abdomen: 10 mSv. Radiation worker limit: 20 mSv/year (5-year average). Acute radiation syndrome threshold: ~1 Sv whole body.
A 200 MBq ⁹⁹ᵐTc bone scan delivers ~4 mSv effective dose. Confuse 4 mSv with 4 rem (40 mSv) and you overstate radiation risk by 10× — potentially delaying a diagnostic scan the patient needs.
Gy is absorbed. Sv is biological-equivalent. rad and rem are the legacy CGS versions, each 100× smaller.

faqs.a: Only for photons and electrons (w_R = 1). Alpha particles: 1 Gy = 20 Sv. Neutrons: 1 Gy = 5–20 Sv.

faqs.q: What's the difference between equivalent and effective dose?
faqs.a: Equivalent dose is per organ, weighted by radiation type. Effective dose is whole-body, further weighted by organ sensitivity.
